title: Taking one piece out
objectives: Design an ablation that removes one change at a time, and read which change mattered.

screens.title: Three changes at once
screens.prose: Our spiral net again, ten seeds a row. The full set-up makes three changes to the baseline at once: Adam instead of SGD, layer norm before each tanh, and dropout 0.1 after it.
screens.question: Which change did the work?

options.text: Adam: the optimiser matters most on a hard problem
options.why: A plausible guess, but both rows moved all three changes at once, so they cannot single Adam out.

options.text: Layer norm: it keeps the tanh units out of saturation
options.why: Plausible again, but these two rows cannot separate layer norm from the other two.

options.text: Dropout: regularising is what lowered the validation loss
options.why: These rows changed dropout together with the rest, so they say nothing about it alone.

options.text: These two rows cannot say: all three changed together

hints.text: How many settings differ between the two rows?
Three changes moved together.
To credit one change, a row must differ from another in that change alone.

feedback.correct: Two rows that differ in three ways cannot rank the three.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count what differs between the rows.

byKey.adam: Adam moved with two other changes.
byKey.ln: Layer norm moved with two other changes.
byKey.do: Dropout moved with two other changes.

explain.text: The loss fell from 0.205 to 0.045, but any mix of the three changes could explain it. To find out, take one change out at a time.

screens.title: Take one out
screens.prose: Each bar is the full set-up with one change taken out, ten seeds each, the same seeds in every bar. The dashed line is the full set-up.
screens.question: Tap the change whose removal raised the loss most.

hints.text: Compare each bar with the dashed line.
The tallest bar shows the costliest removal.
Without layer norm the loss is 0.157.

feedback.correct: Taking out layer norm costs most: 0.157 against 0.045.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the tallest bar.

byKey.noadam: Removing Adam raised the loss to 0.103; removing layer norm raised it more.
byKey.nodo: Removing dropout lowered the loss to 0.022: dropout was costing us.
byKey.full: That bar is the full set-up itself.

explain.text: Layer norm matters most here, Adam next. Removing dropout lowers the loss to 0.022, so on this small net dropout was hurting.

screens.title: An ablation
screens.prose: What you just read is an **ablation**: start from the full set-up, remove one change at a time, and measure each row across the same seeds. The effect of a change is the mean, over seeds, of (loss without it) minus (loss of the full set-up).
screens.question: What is the effect of dropout, by that definition? Give 3 decimal places, with its sign.

hints.text: Loss without dropout, minus the full set-up's loss.
The two bars are 0.022 and 0.045.
The result is negative: removing dropout helped.

feedback.correct: $0.0217 - 0.0453 = -0.0236$: dropout made the loss worse by about 0.024.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Take the full set-up's loss from the loss without dropout.

byKey.sign: You subtracted the other way round. Without minus full is negative here.
byKey.level: That is the loss without dropout; subtract the full set-up's.

explain.text: Without dropout the loss is 0.0217, against 0.0453 with it. The effect is -0.0236: negative, so the change hurt. A positive effect means the full set-up needs the change.

screens.title: Reading a removal table
screens.prose: The removal table: for each change, the mean over ten seeds of (without it) minus (full), and the sd of those ten differences.
screens.question: Put the changes in order, the one the full set-up needs most first.

hints.text: A bigger positive effect means a costlier removal.
The effects are 0.111, 0.058 and -0.024.
Negative comes last: the set-up is better without it.

feedback.correct: Layer norm, then Adam; dropout has a negative effect.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Sort by the effect, largest first.

byKey.adam: Adam's effect, 0.058, is smaller than layer norm's.
byKey.do: Dropout's effect is negative, so it goes last.

explain.text: Removing layer norm costs 0.111 and removing Adam 0.058, with sds of 0.047 and 0.066 across seeds. Adam's effect is noisy: its sd exceeds its mean. Dropout's -0.024 is small but steady.

screens.title: Adding one at a time
screens.prose: The other direction adds one change at a time to the baseline. With dropout left out, here are the four mixes of Adam and layer norm, ten seeds each.
screens.question: How much does switching to Adam lower the loss, without layer norm and with it? Give 3 decimal places.

hints.text: Compare the two rows within one column.
Without layer norm: 0.205 to 0.084.
With layer norm: 0.086 to 0.022.

feedback.correct: 0.121 without layer norm, 0.064 with it: the gains differ.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Take the Adam loss from the SGD loss in each column.

byKey.sign0: A gain is the SGD loss minus the Adam loss.
byKey.sign1: A gain is the SGD loss minus the Adam loss.

explain.text: Adam changes the loss by $-0.121$ without layer norm and by $-0.064$ with it. The **interaction** is $I = -0.064 - (-0.121) = 0.057$: positive, because the two changes overlap. So the two directions can measure a change differently: Adam is worth 0.121 added to the baseline and 0.058 removed from the full set-up.

screens.title: How many runs
screens.prose: A remove-one ablation needs the full set-up plus one row per change, each over the same seeds.
screens.question: How many training runs does our ablation of three changes with 10 seeds need, the full set-up included?

hints.text: Count the rows, then multiply by the seeds.
Four rows: the full set-up and three removals.

byKey.nofull: You left out the full set-up's own ten runs.
byKey.fact: That is every mix of the three changes, $2^3 \times 10$; remove-one needs fewer.

explain.text: Changes plus one, times seeds: $(3 + 1) \times 10 = 40$. Adding the add-one direction brings in the baseline and three more rows; with three changes that happens to be all $2^3 = 8$ mixes, 80 runs.

screens.title: One seed each
screens.prose: A colleague runs the ablation with seed 6 only. Removing Adam costs 0.237 and removing layer norm 0.118. Their slide says "Adam is the key change".
screens.question: What should you tell them?

options.text: Seed 6 is one draw; over ten seeds layer norm's removal costs more (0.111 against 0.058)
Agreed: on seed 6 removing Adam costs 0.237, about twice layer norm's
options.why: You ranked the changes on one seed, where the ranking is a draw like any other.

options.text: Remove Adam and layer norm together in one row, to save runs
options.why: A row that changes two things cannot credit either one.

hints.text: How much do single-seed differences vary?
Adam's removal effect has an sd of 0.066 across seeds.
Rank on the mean over seeds.

feedback.correct: One seed per row makes the "most important" change partly noise.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask how big the seed-to-seed spread is.

byKey.agree: One seed per row can reorder the changes.
byKey.both: Changing two things in one row confounds them.

explain.text: Seed 6 happens to make SGD look bad: removing Adam there costs 0.237, against a mean of 0.058. Over ten seeds layer norm's removal costs more on average, 0.111 against 0.058. Ablate across seeds, one change per row.

screens.title: Edge case: helps only with another
screens.prose: Suppose another net gives these means over ten seeds: base 0.300, a wider layer alone 0.310, dropout alone 0.290, both 0.240. The wider layer hurts on its own. Each difference has an sd of about 0.01 across the ten seeds.
screens.question: Dropout is on. Adding the wider layer changes the loss by how much? Give 3 decimal places, with its sign.

hints.text: Stay in the dropout column.
Wider with dropout minus narrow with dropout.

feedback.correct: $0.240 - 0.290 = -0.050$: with dropout the wider layer helps.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare the two rows in the dropout column.

byKey.alone: That is its effect without dropout, where it hurts.
byKey.sign: That is the removal effect, without minus with; the question asks with minus without.

explain.text: Without dropout the wider layer adds 0.010; with dropout it removes 0.050. A remove-one ablation from the full set-up credits it with 0.050, and an add-one ablation calls it harmful. Both are true: it helps only alongside dropout.

screens.title: The rule
screens.prose: One change per row, every row on the same $n$ seeds. $L_{ab}$ is the mean loss with change A off (0) or on (1) and change B off or on. You measured each change by taking it out, and an interaction from a 2 by 2 table: $$\Delta_k = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{s=1}^{n}\big(L_s(\text{full} - k) - L_s(\text{full})\big), \qquad I = (L_{11} - L_{01}) - (L_{10} - L_{00}).$$
screens.question: An ablation row shows $\Delta_k = -0.03$. What does that say about change $k$?

options.text: Taking it out lowered the loss: the full set-up is better without it
It is the most valuable change, since its effect is largest in size
options.why: The sign matters: a negative effect means the loss fell when the change was removed.

options.text: It did nothing, since the effect is below zero
options.why: Below zero is not zero: the loss moved, downwards, when the change came out.

feedback.correct: A negative effect means the change was costing the full set-up.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the sign of without minus full.

byKey.nothing: Negative is a real move, not none.

explain.text: Without minus full is negative, so the loss fell when $k$ was removed. As with our dropout, the change was hurting, at least on these seeds.

screens.title: An ablation table in code
screens.prose: Write `ablation_table(runs, full, removed)`: for each change, pair each seed of the row without it with the same seed of `full`, and return the mean and sd ($n - 1$) of the differences. Then `interaction(t)` for a 2 by 2 table of mean losses.
screens.question: Write both functions.

Subtracts the other way round, so the signs flip.
Pairs by list position, so out-of-order seeds are mismatched.
Takes the interaction as both changes against the base.

hints.text: Key the full set-up's losses by seed first.
Pair by seed number, not by position in the list.

feedback.correct: All pass. Our table reads 0.0577, 0.1112 and -0.0236 for Adam, layer norm and dropout.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the first failing test in the results.

screens.title: Before the capital moves
screens.prose: A quant team's new return model adds five features and a new loss to last year's model, and its backtest is better. The head of research asks for a remove-one ablation, each row trained with 5 seeds.
screens.question: How many training runs is that, the full model included?

hints.text: Count the changes: features and the loss.
Six changes, so seven rows.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the changes, add the full row, multiply by the seeds.

byKey.nofull: You left out the full model's own runs.
byKey.five: The new loss is a change too.
byKey.fact: That is every mix, $2^6 \times 5$; remove-one needs far fewer.

explain.text: Five features and a loss are six changes, so seven rows of 5 seeds: 35 runs. Each feature's row shows what it adds on top of the rest, with a seed spread to judge it by.

ideas: An ablation removes one change at a time from the full set-up, each row over the same seeds, and reports the mean difference and its sd.
On our net layer norm mattered most (0.111), Adam next (0.058), and dropout hurt (-0.024).
Changes interact: adding one to the baseline and removing it from the full set-up can disagree, so say which direction you ran.

formula.name: Ablation effect and interaction
formula.note: Paired by seed; one change per row.

summary.trap: One seed per row, or two changes in one row: the "most important" change is then partly noise or confounded.

quiz.prose: A remove-one ablation tests four changes, each row over 3 seeds.
quiz.question: How many training runs, the full set-up included?

byKey.nofull: The full set-up needs its own runs.

explain.text: Four removals plus the full set-up make 5 rows, and $5 \times 3 = 15$ runs.

quiz.prose: A removal table reads: change P, effect 0.040 (sd 0.005); change Q, effect 0.045 (sd 0.090), over ten seeds each.
quiz.question: Which change does the evidence support more firmly?

options.text: P: its effect is steady across seeds
Q: its effect is the larger of the two
options.why: Q's mean is a little larger, but its sd is twice its mean, so its sign is uncertain.

options.text: Neither: the effects are almost equal
options.why: The means are close, but the spreads differ eighteenfold.

feedback.correct: P's ten differences all sit near 0.040; Q's swing either way.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare each effect with its sd.

explain.text: An effect counts only against its seed spread. P's 0.040 has sd 0.005; Q's 0.045 has sd 0.090, so some seeds show Q hurting.

quiz.prose: Mean losses: base 0.50; with change A 0.40; with change B 0.45; with both 0.30.
quiz.question: What is the interaction: A's effect with B on, minus its effect with B off? Give 2 decimal places, with its sign.

feedback.generic: Not quite. A's effect in each column, then the difference.

byKey.sign: Keep the order: with B on minus with B off.
byKey.both: That is both changes against the base.

explain.text: A lowers the loss by 0.10 alone and by 0.15 with B. The interaction is $-0.15 - (-0.10) = -0.05$: the two help more together.
